key_terms.meaning: An analytical device that pairs a biological recognition element with a transducer to give a measurable signal proportional to one analyte
The biological part (enzyme, antibody, nucleic acid, cell, receptor) that binds or reacts with only the target analyte
The physical part that converts the biological event into an electrical signal: current, voltage, light or mass change
Plot of signal (y) against known standard concentrations (x); slope = sensitivity, intercept = background
Lowest concentration giving signal larger than blank by a fixed margin, often blank mean + 3 × standard deviation of blank
Ability to respond to the target while ignoring similar molecules such as other sugars or other proteins
Substrate concentration at which enzyme rate is half of Vmax; sets the upper useful range of an enzyme sensor
Measurement of current at a fixed electrode potential; current is proportional to the concentration of electroactive species
Measurement of voltage at near-zero current; voltage follows the Nernst equation, about 59 mV per decade at 25 °C
Fixing the enzyme or antibody onto the electrode surface by adsorption, covalent bonding, cross-linking or entrapment
Ion-sensitive field-effect transistor: a MOSFET whose metal gate is replaced by ion-selective membrane plus sample, so surface charge shifts threshold voltage
Gate voltage at which the MOSFET channel just forms; in an ISFET it moves with the charge on the membrane surface
Immunologically sensitive FET: antibody layer on the gate; antigen binding changes charge and shifts VT
Needle enzyme electrode left in interstitial fluid for days, giving a reading every few minutes, with a lag of roughly 5–15 minutes behind blood
Pairing of a single-stranded probe with its complementary target strand to form a double helix
One-molecule-thick ordered film, typically an alkanethiol on gold, used to attach probes and block bare surface
Hairpin DNA with a redox tag at one end; hybridisation opens the stem, moves the tag away from the electrode and lowers the current
Distance over which a surface charge is screened by ions in solution; about 0.7–0.8 nm in 150 mM salt
Semiconductor nanocrystal (for example CdSe) whose emission colour is set by particle size, used as an optical or electrochemical label
Size- and shape-dependent light absorption of metal nanoparticles that shifts when molecules bind to their surface

takeaways: A biosensor is only a system: recognition element, transducer and electronics, and no reading is trusted until it is calibrated against standards.
Selectivity comes from the biological element; the usable range and detection limit come from its binding or catalytic kinetics.
Electrochemical transducers are popular because they are cheap, small and give a direct electrical signal that a simple circuit can digitise.
In an ISFET the sample itself acts as part of the gate, so the measured quantity is a shift in threshold voltage, not a current through a membrane.
The disposable glucose strip is the most widely used biosensor in the world, and the continuous monitor turns the same chemistry into a time trace.
DNA biosensors trade the enzyme's amplification for sequence specificity, and read the amount of duplex formed by current or impedance.
At the nanoscale, high surface area amplifies small binding events, but charge screening by salt limits what can be detected electrically.
bank_note: Long answers here usually begin with the recognition-element–transducer pair, then move to calibration, limit of detection and controls, and finish with one worked device such as the glucose strip, the ISFET or the DNA electrode.

bank.q: Define a biosensor. Name its three essential components and state the function of each, with one medical and one environmental example.
outline: Definition linking biological recognition to a measurable signal proportional to one analyte
Bio-recognition element: enzyme, antibody, nucleic acid, cell or receptor
Transducer: electrochemical, optical, piezoelectric or thermal
Electronics: amplification, digitisation, display
Example: glucose strip (medical); pesticide or BOD sensor (environment)

bank.q: Explain how a biosensor differs from an ordinary chemical or physical sensor, and why the biological element is the source of selectivity.
outline: Physical sensor responds to a bulk property; chemical sensor responds to a class of species
Biological element gives molecular recognition through shape and charge complementarity
Enzyme active site, antigen–antibody fit, base pairing
Selectivity measured against interfering species
Selectivity does not fix range or LOD; kinetics do

bank.q: Classify biosensors by bio-recognition element and by transducer type, giving one example of each class.
outline: By recognition: enzyme, antibody, DNA, cell, microbial, aptamer
By transducer: amperometric, potentiometric, conductometric, optical, piezoelectric, calorimetric
Calorimetric and piezoelectric explained in one line each
Example device for each class
Note that a single analyte can be measured by more than one class

bank.q: Explain Michaelis–Menten kinetics and show how Km and Vmax set the useful measuring range of an enzyme electrode.
outline: Rate equation and meaning of Vmax and Km
First-order region at low substrate, zero-order at high substrate
Linear range sits where signal is proportional to concentration
Immobilisation lowers activity and can shift apparent Km
Diffusion limitation in a thick film widens or narrows the range
Link to detection limit and saturation point

bank.q: Describe the structure and principle of an ISFET, and explain how it differs from a MOSFET.
outline: MOSFET structure: source, drain, gate oxide, metal gate
ISFET: metal gate replaced by ion-selective membrane, sample and reference electrode
Surface charge on membrane changes threshold voltage
Nernstian response, about 59 mV per pH unit at 25 °C
Difference: input is ionic activity in solution, not a gate voltage
Drift and reference electrode issues

bank.q: A glucose sensor gives readings of 12, 26, 51, 98 and 190 nA for standards of 1, 2, 4, 8 and 16 mmol/L. Find the sensitivity and, if the blank gives 3.0 ± 0.6 nA, the limit of detection.
outline: Plot or fit signal against concentration; slope in nA per mmol/L
Sensitivity from slope, check linearity and intercept
Blank signal plus 3 × standard deviation of blank
Convert that signal to concentration using the slope
State LOD with units
Comment on whether the standard addition method is needed for a real sample matrix

bank.q: Design a disposable amperometric glucose sensor strip for a home meter. Choose the enzyme, the immobilisation method, the electrode material, the applied potential and the calibration scheme, and justify each choice.
outline: Glucose oxidase or dehydrogenase; reaction producing H2O2 or using a mediator
Immobilisation by cross-linking or entrapment in a printed film
Screen-printed carbon working electrode, Ag/AgCl reference
Potential about 0.6–0.7 V for H2O2, or lower with a mediator
Nafion or similar membrane to cut interference from uric acid and ascorbate
Two-point calibration per strip batch, coding, fingerstick confirmatory tests

bank.q: An ISFET with a Nernstian slope of 59 mV per pH unit is used for a urea sensor. Calculate the threshold shift for a pH change of 0.05 and explain two reasons a measured shift may not match this figure.
outline: Sign follows direction of pH change
Reason 1: membrane drift and hydration over hours
Reason 2: reference electrode instability or junction potential
Reason 3: incomplete urease conversion at low urea or short residence time
Calibration and blank correction before any reading is quoted

bank.q: Design a DNA biosensor to detect a known single-base mutation. Describe the probe, its attachment, the hybridisation step, the signal readout, the controls and the stringency wash.
outline: Short probe matched to the mutant sequence, 15–30 bases
Thiol probe on gold through a self-assembled monolayer, backfilled to control spacing
Hybridisation in buffer at chosen salt and temperature
Readout: redox label, intercalator current, or impedance change
Positive control target, negative control mismatched target, blank
Stringency wash: raised temperature or lowered salt melts mismatched duplex
Single-base discrimination demonstrated by comparing signals

bank.q: A home test uses gold nanoparticles with an antibody sandwich for a cardiac marker. Explain how the LSPR signal arises, why nanoparticles amplify small binding events, and what limits the test.
outline: LSPR absorption depends on particle size, shape and spacing
Binding of antigen and second antibody layer changes local refractive index
Shift in wavelength or colour change read by eye or simple optics
Optical readout avoids charge screening by salt
Limits: antibody cross-reactivity, matrix effects in whole blood, batch-to-batch particle size, quantitation accuracy

bank.q: A continuous glucose monitor reads 4.2 mmol/L while the fingerstick reads 6.0 mmol/L on day 6 of wear, with the gap widening after meals. Analyse the likely causes and state how calibration and alarms should be handled.
outline: Interstitial fluid lag behind blood, exaggerated by rising or falling glucose
Sensor drift and enzyme decay over wear time
Pressure-induced changes in local perfusion at night
Calibration: fingerstick calibration points, time limits on calibration validity
Trend arrows rather than single points; alarms set on rate of change
Accuracy expressed as mean absolute relative difference against reference
Rule that a reading is confirmed with a fingerstick before dosing

bank.q: Compare an enzyme electrode, an ISFET and a nanomaterial FET as the basis of a portable urea meter. Judge which you would choose for a clinic and give reasons.
outline: Enzyme electrode: urease converts urea to ammonium, amperometric or potentiometric readout, cheap and proven
ISFET: label-free, small, but drift and reference electrode problems
Nanomaterial FET: high sensitivity, but Debye screening in high-salt samples and reproducibility issues
Criteria: detection limit, linear range in urine, drift, sterility, cost per test, calibration burden
Recommendation with a stated trade-off
Controls and calibration plan for the chosen device

bank.q: Explain how Debye screening restricts label-free electrical detection of charged molecules, and analyse three ways to overcome it.
outline: Debye length about 0.7–0.8 nm in 150 mM salt; charge beyond it is screened from the electrode
Consequence: large targets and whole cells give weak signal in serum
Strategy: dilute the sample to lengthen Debye length
Strategy: move the binding event close to the surface, using short probes or fragmented targets
Strategy: use an optical or mass readout that ignores charge screening
State cost of each strategy: loss of sample realism or added steps

bank.q: Judge labelled versus label-free DNA detection for a fever panel that must run without a thermocycler.
outline: Labelled route: redox tag, intercalator or fluorophore; higher signal, extra washing steps
Sandwich format for longer targets and extra specificity
Label-free route: impedance or FET; simpler chemistry, more sensitive to matrix
E-DNA stem-loop gives reagentless, reusable sensing but single-step kinetics
Throughput, cost per test in rupees, shelf life, need for controls
Verdict tied to the stated requirement of no thermocycler

glossary.def: The specific substance the biosensor is built to measure.
Sensor that holds the electrode at a fixed potential and measures the resulting current.
Sensor that measures voltage at almost zero current, usually with an ion-selective membrane.
Electrode of known, stable potential, usually Ag/AgCl, against which the sensing electrode is measured.
Electrode where the reaction of interest is driven and the current is measured.
Small redox molecule that shuttles electrons from an enzyme to the electrode, allowing a lower operating potential.
Enzyme sensor that measures the natural substrate or product, such as oxygen or hydrogen peroxide.
Enzyme sensor that uses a mediator or redox dye to transfer electrons instead of relying on oxygen.
Sensor in which the enzyme transfers electrons directly to the electrode without a mediator.
Amount of substrate converted per unit time under stated conditions, usually in units per milligram.
Measure of how tightly an antibody binds its antigen; tighter binding lowers the detection limit but slows release.
Format where a capture probe binds the target and a second labelled probe binds a different site on the same target.
Combination of temperature, salt and detergent in a wash that removes mismatched duplexes while keeping perfect matches.
Short single-stranded nucleic acid of known sequence fixed on the sensor surface.
Electroactive group such as ferrocene or methylene blue whose proximity to the electrode changes the measured current.
Technique that measures how the electrode–solution interface resists and stores charge over a range of frequencies.
Relation giving electrode potential as a function of ion activity, about 59 mV per decade at 25 °C for a one-electron change.
Thin film that lets one ion pass or binds it, producing a charge at the surface of an ISFET or electrode.
Reduction of the effect of a surface charge by ions in the surrounding solution.
Permselective polymer film that lets small molecules through while blocking anions such as ascorbate.
Mean absolute relative difference, the usual accuracy measure for a continuous glucose monitor.
Paper-based test where labelled particles move by capillary action and are captured on a test line.
Ability of an implanted sensor to stay in the body without harming tissue or being fouled by it.
Build-up of protein and cells on a sensor surface that blocks the analyte and reduces signal over time.
